identity.title: POCUS cardiac: pericardial effusion (subxiphoid/PLAX), with RA/RV diastolic collapse for tamponade

technique.how: Phased-array probe, subxiphoid 4-chamber and parasternal long-axis views; look for an anechoic stripe between heart and bright pericardium (circumferential if large; <1 cm small, >2 cm large). For tamponade, look for RA collapse in systole, RV free-wall collapse in diastole (M-mode), plethoric non-collapsing IVC and swinging heart.
technique.prerequisites: Operator trained in focused cardiac POCUS; if unstable, scan during resuscitation; correlate with ECG/vitals.

interpretation.positive_finding: Anechoic pericardial fluid separating the visceral and parietal pericardium; with RV diastolic collapse, RA systolic collapse and a plethoric IVC in a hypotensive/tachycardic patient this indicates tamponade physiology.
interpretation.negative_finding: No pericardial fluid in adequate subxiphoid and parasternal views effectively excludes a significant effusion and therefore tamponade as the cause of shock.
interpretation.pitfalls: Epicardial fat pad (anterior, echogenic, moves with the heart) and left pleural effusion (posterior to the descending aorta on PLAX) mimic effusion. Chamber collapse is insensitive/nonspecific in pulmonary hypertension, RV hypertrophy, loculated post-surgical effusions and hypovolemia; tamponade remains a clinical diagnosis.
interpretation.changes_what: Effusion with hypotension and RA/RV collapse or plethoric IVC: treat as tamponade (fluids as bridge, urgent pericardiocentesis/cardiology); no effusion removes tamponade from the shock differential.

estimates.target_condition: Pericardial effusion (detection by emergency-physician bedside echocardiography)
estimates.population: 515 ED patients meeting high-risk criteria for pericardial effusion (103 with effusion); emergency physicians trained in ultrasonography
estimates.reference_standard: Review of all captured images by the Department of Cardiology
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.96/(1-0.98) = 48; LR- = (1-0.96)/0.98 = 0.041, from sensitivity 96% and specificity 98%; prevalence 103/515
estimates.quote: Emergency physicians detected pericardial effusion with a sensitivity of 96% (95% confidence interval [CI] 90.4% to 98.9%), specificity of 98% (95% CI 95.8% to 99.1%)

estimates.target_condition: Pericardial effusion (eFAST pericardial view in trauma)
estimates.population: Trauma patients undergoing eFAST; pooled from 75 studies/24,350 patients overall (pericardial subset not separately sized in abstract)
estimates.reference_standard: CT, formal echocardiography or operative findings per included studies
estimates.quote: Pooled sensitivities and specificities were calculated for the detection of pneumothorax (69% and 99% respectively), pericardial effusion (91% and 94% respectively)

sources.citation: Mandavia DP, Hoffner RJ, Mahaney K, Henderson SO. Bedside echocardiography by emergency physicians. Ann Emerg Med. 2001;38(4):377-382.
Netherton S, Milenkovic V, Taylor M, Davis PJ. Diagnostic accuracy of eFAST in the trauma patient: a systematic review and meta-analysis. CJEM. 2019;21(6):727-738.

Merce J, Sagrista-Sauleda J, Permanyer-Miralda G, Evangelista A, Soler-Soler J. Correlation between clinical and Doppler echocardiographic findings in patients with moderate and large pericardial effusion: implications for the diagnosis of cardiac tamponade. Am Heart J. 1999;138(4 Pt 1):759-764.
Roy CL, Minor MA, Brookhart MA, Choudhry NK. Does this patient with a pericardial effusion have cardiac tamponade? JAMA. 2007;297(16):1810-1818.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not diagnose tamponade from chamber collapse alone in a normotensive patient, and do not exclude it on the basis of absent collapse in pulmonary hypertension, RV hypertrophy or loculated/post-cardiac-surgery effusions.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Effusion with hypotension, tachycardia, elevated JVP or pulsus paradoxus >10 mm Hg is tamponade until proven otherwise: call cardiology/perform pericardiocentesis urgently and avoid positive-pressure ventilation if possible.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Mandavia 2001 used cardiology over-read of all EP images as the standard (overall accuracy 97.5%); no kappa reported in the abstract. Merce 1999 shows RA collapse is sensitive but nonspecific (68%/66%) and RV collapse specific but insensitive.
safety_scope.skill_assumption: Assumes an operator credentialed in focused cardiac POCUS (subxiphoid and PLAX windows, effusion vs fat pad vs pleural fluid, M-mode for RV diastolic collapse); Mandavia's operators were ultrasound-trained emergency physicians, and tamponade signs require more advanced skill than effusion detection.

extraction_notes: Mandavia 2001 (Ann Emerg Med, not open access) sensitivity/specificity with CIs are in the abstract; LRs computed from point estimates and flagged. Netherton 2019 eFAST pooled pericardial estimate from abstract (no CIs in abstract). Merce 1999 tamponade-sign estimates use CLINICAL tamponade as the reference standard (reverse of usual design) - interpret as concordance rather than accuracy; RA-collapse values (68%/66%) not entered as a separate estimate to keep quotes within 25 words but are noted here; setting recorded as mixed (single-center cardiology cohort, inpatient/outpatient not stated). Roy 2007 JAMA RCE cited for clinical context (pulsus paradoxus >10 mm Hg LR 3.3) but no POCUS estimate; that number is a physical-exam finding and not entered here.
